Kedainiai Jewish Cemetery Oldest Part

Jewish Cemetery · Kauno apskritis, Lithuania

Demolished. Kėdainiai — known in Yiddish as Keidan — was one of the most significant Jewish spiritual centers in Lithuania: the legendary Vilna Gaon himself studied Torah and Talmud here under the local rabbi Moses Margalioth, and the town's community held a respected, founding place in the Va'ad Medinat Lita, the autonomous council governing Lithuanian Jewry from 1623 to 1764, hosting gatherings of representatives from every Lithuanian Jewish community in 1778 and 1782. The community was also known for its farming families — at least 80 households cultivated the region's famously exported cucumbers — and, before WWII, supported seven prayer houses, three of which still stand today, in good condition, repurposed for cultural use. On August 28, 1941, 2,076 Jews from Kėdainiai and its surrounding areas were murdered in ditches near the Smilga River; a 2011 memorial identifies 1,003 of the victims by name. This is the oldest of what was once a single, larger cemetery, later divided into several separately protected sections; it is now completely empty, marked only by a memorial stone, while a separately documented newer section nearby holds about 600 surviving gravestones.
